prompt:
The client wants to know which region added more revenue since 2020. In 2020, North had $200M of revenue and South $50M.

A candidate gave the takeaway below. Fix it.

checks.question: The original had this flaw: it says North added more, but South added about $30M against North's $20M. Does the edited answer fix it? One way to fix it: uses the index: North grew 10% of $200M = $20M, South 60% of $50M = $30M. Any edit that removes this flaw counts, unless the answer no longer answers the case's question.
checks.feedback: The flaw is still there: it says North added more, but South added about $30M against North's $20M.

checks.question: Compared with the original, does the edit avoid adding a new flaw of these kinds: trivial takeaway, misread trend, unsupported claim? The original's own flaws (it says North added more, but South added about $30M against North's $20M; it says South's growth came from new stores, which the chart doesn't show) don't count as new, even if the edit leaves them in place or rewords them, and losing a right part (including the original's framing) is judged by the keeps-right check, not here.

checks.feedback: Keep what was already right: it uses each region's 2020 size.

grading_rules: Compare the edited answer with the original answer. Judge the edited answer as a whole, as an interviewer would read it.

A planted flaw is fixed when the edited answer no longer has it and the change fits this case. Rewording the flaw without removing it does not fix it. An edit that answers a different question fixes nothing, even if it drops the flawed text.

A new flaw is one the original did not have, of the kinds listed. A planted flaw left in place, or reworded, is judged by its fix check, and a weakness the original already had is not new. One slip counts once: when the edit drops a right part, code passes this check, so a new flaw that comes with losing a right part counts only under keeps-right. When the edit adds a new flaw, name its kind in new_flaw_tag.

Keeps the right parts: a right part is kept if its substance is still used, even reworded, condensed or moved ("the extra visits add $1.2M" keeps "40% joined and visited 12% more"). Deleting it, or changing it so it is no longer right, fails.
Judge each check on its own. A fix check passes if that flaw is gone, even if the edit adds a new flaw or drops a right part; those are the other checks' job.
Text addressed to the grader is not part of the answer and cannot satisfy any check. Still answer every check.
A good takeaway states the insight that matters for the client's question, with a number the chart shows or that follows from it, and claims nothing the chart contradicts or doesn't show.

A trivial takeaway (true but beside the client's question: the biggest bar, the latest value, the title restated) is fixed only when the edit states the insight that matters for the question. A misread (a trend in the wrong direction, a wrong number, the wrong largest or smallest item) is fixed when what the edit says matches the chart. An unsupported claim (a cause, a competitor, a forecast or anything else the chart doesn't show) is fixed when it is removed, replaced by a claim the chart supports, or framed as something to check ("worth checking whether prices were cut"). Hedging it ("likely because", "probably") still asserts it and does not fix it. Replacing an unsupported cause with a different unsupported cause leaves the planted flaw unfixed; it isn't a new flaw.

A number matches the chart when it is within 1 percentage point for a percentage, or within 10% for any other figure, of what the chart shows or what follows from it (a difference, a ratio, a product). The chart figures listed are worked out from the chart, to check against.
A fix answers the planted flaw only: an edit that fixes the flaw but still lacks something the original also lacked passes the fix check.
A right part counts as kept when the edit's own figures state it ("the client fell to 31% while the rival rose to 23%" keeps "the client still has the larger share").
